entries.title: M John Harrison becomes first science fiction author to win the Booker prize
entries.summary: The 81-year-old’s postapocalyptic novel The End of Everything takes home the £50,000 awardGuardian fiction editor Justine Jordan on M John Harrison’s win: A visionary writer gets the recognition he deservesEighty-one-year-old M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, a postapocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast, becoming the oldest winner in the award’s history
entries.content:
Eighty-one-year-old M John Harrison has won the Booker prize for The End of Everything, a postapocalyptic novel set on a near-future Kent coast, becoming the oldest winner in the award’s history.

Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said that while plenty of previous winners had dabbled in science fiction, Harrison’s was “the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world”. She called it “a historic win, for a writer whose decades of work are lightly worn on every page”.

Harrison, who has been publishing for six decades, overtakes Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she shared the prize in 2019 for The Testaments. He received the £50,000 award and trophy at a ceremony in London on Monday evening.

The End of Everything, Harrison’s first Booker nomination, is set a few decades from now, years after a disaster nobody can properly account for. Set on the Kent coast, the novel sees Phillip Tennent and his ageing aunt Marnie attempting to survive alongside the looming threat of the mysterious iGhetti: vast, shape-changing beings whose origins and intentions are never explained. At 198 pages, it was the shortest book on the shortlist.

Mary Beard, chair of the judges, said the decision was unanimous, reached after a full day of discussion. “It’s a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile – and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism,” she said. “One main point of the book is that if, or when, such an apocalypse comes it will be incomprehensible. And the old rules won’t matter either … This is the politics of now seen through the lens of the future.”

Harrison, born in Rugby, Warwickshire, in 1945, sold his first story in 1965 and spent most of the 1970s running the books pages of the speculative fiction magazine New Worlds. Alongside his novels he has written five short-story collections and the “anti-memoir” Wish I Was Here (2023). Climbers took the Boardman Tasker prize for mountain literature in 1989, Nova Swing the Arthur C Clarke award in 2007, and The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again the Goldsmiths prize in 2020. Once a keen climber and fell runner, he sat on the Booker judging panel in 2022.

This year’s shortlist included two former winners: Marlon James, the bookmakers’ favourite, for The Disappearers, and Douglas Stuart for John of John. Elizabeth Strout’s The Things We Never Say, Luke Kennard’s Black Bag and Rebecca Perry’s debut May We Feed the King completed the list. Each shortlisted author receives £2,500.

Writing in the Guardian on his inspiration last week, Harrison described The End of Everything as “a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend”, with aliens who arrive “as incomers from another dimension, paralleling the gentrification of places like the UK’s south-east coast”. He admitted to passing on to the reader “some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters”, but said he hoped the issues were transparent – among them “the collapse of rationality that comes with Trumpism and the internet”.

His win marks a rare moment of mainstream recognition for a writer long revered by his peers but at the margins of literary fiction. On BBC Radio 4’s Front Row last month, Harrison said he had been “working for 40 to 50 years to shift the balance, both as a novelist and as a critic”, adding: “Why shouldn’t a well written [work of] SF be considered to be literary fiction?”

Even admirers concede the book is not an easy read. In a rave review for the Guardian, Michel Faber said it “exposes the terrifying insecurity of life right now”, but warned that “it won’t be for everyone”.

The win is timely in the age of AI. Beard noted that the “i” in iGhetti hints “at something digital, but you can’t be sure”, while Wood described the book’s post-apocalyptic landscape as “Large Language Model-dotted”.

The judging panel also included Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, authors Patricia Lockwood and Raymond Antrobus and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu. They considered 163 books published in the UK or Ireland between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026.

It is the first Booker win for Serpent’s Tail, an imprint of the independent publisher Profile Books, and its fifth nomination. Hungarian-British author David Szalay won last year with Flesh; other recent winners include Samantha Harvey’s Orbital, Paul Lynch’s Prophet Song and Shehan Karunatilaka’s The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida.

  • The End of Everything by M. John Harrison (Profile, £16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: Jarvis Cocker on judging the Booker prize: ‘It’s just like being in a band’
entries.summary: The singer on how being in Pulp prepared him for judging a literary prize, reading 163 books while on tour, and feeling like the odd one out on the panel• M John Harrison becomes the first science fiction author to win the Booker prizeJudging the Booker prize is like being in a band. A band will often bring together a very disparate set of people, their only thing in common the fact they’re in the
entries.content:
Judging the Booker prize is like being in a band. A band will often bring together a very disparate set of people, their only thing in common the fact they’re in the same group. And a good band takes account of the interests and strengths of its members – that’s how you get a unique sound. Being part of this year’s Booker prize judging panel – chaired by Mary Beard, and featuring the writers Patricia Lockwood, Raymond Antrobus and Rebecca Liu – felt much the same. We were all very different, but we had a common cause: to pick a good winner.

Both bands and Booker prize panels are, at least ostensibly, democracies (though in Pulp, I’m the singer, so I make more noise than everybody else). But they shouldn’t be bland democracies. Mary didn’t expect us to toe a party line, and our panel managed to avoid what can sometimes happen when you’re on a jury and you end up agreeing on the least offensive option.

Walking into the final judging meeting last Saturday, I had three books in mind that I would have been happy to see win, but I had no idea who we’d land on. We seesawed around quite a lot, and it took a while, but we eventually managed to settle on a winner. And no scones were thrown at each other in the process.

We agreed that The End of Everything by M John Harrison is not a particularly easy book to read. But that’s not because it’s badly written – it’s actually very well written. The author is telling us that the thing that has gone wrong with the world is something that no one can really understand. For too many readers, Harrison has flown under the radar – this book is a culmination of his craft.

I judged the Booker prize while touring – the 163 eligible novels helped fill long, usually very boring flights. I couldn’t lug around a massive bag of books, so I had to read them on my iPad. I wouldn’t recommend it as a reading experience, but in this case it did help me be fairly objective – I couldn’t be put off by a rubbish cover. I also wasn’t aware of the author’s name when I was reading a book, meaning any conscious or unconscious prejudices that I may have had towards them disappeared. I sometimes had to do a judging meeting while on tour – when in Sydney, the time difference meant one of the sessions ran from 1am to 3am (luckily it wasn’t the night we played).

I ended up reading The End of Everything three times. During the re-reading process, some of the books deepened – you saw bits that you missed on the first read – and others shallowed out – you felt like you’d got everything the first time round.

Going into the process, I was worried it would put me off reading. I also felt, rightly or wrongly, like I was the least qualified judge – the odd one out on a panel of established writers and industry professionals. So in some ways I’m surprised I enjoyed it so much. I’m definitely never going to read 163 books in a year again, but I’ve certainly become a faster reader – I now finish a book in three or four days (though I don’t know if that’ll last, or if I’ll slow down to my usual tortoiselike pace again). And I’ve discovered contemporary writers I love, who I’ll continue to follow.

I’d never been in a book club before this; reading had always been a solitary pursuit. But in the way that reading a book is sometimes a welcome relief from your own consciousness, listening to what the other judges, with different modes of life, had to say about the books was fascinating. Anyone who’s invited to be a Booker prize judge is in for a treat.

entries.title: Lessons in Harmony by Jonathan Coe review – what can music tell us about national identity?
entries.summary: The unlikely friendship between French and English composers Maurice Ravel and Ralph Vaughan Williams has inspired a tender and generous novelIn 1907, composer Ralph Vaughan Williams confided to the critic Edwin Evans that he was finding his own music “lumpy and stodgy”. His musical education at the Royal College of Music, and indeed classical music in England in general at that time, had tended t
entries.content:
In 1907, composer Ralph Vaughan Williams confided to the critic Edwin Evans that he was finding his own music “lumpy and stodgy”. His musical education at the Royal College of Music, and indeed classical music in England in general at that time, had tended towards the Teutonic – Bach, Brahms, Beethoven, Wagner – and their heavy contrapuntal style dominated his work. To free himself, he told Evans, he planned to spend some months studying under French composer Vincent d’Indy, who taught at the Paris Conservatoire. Evans’s colleague, Michel-Dimitri Calvocoressi, had other ideas. He proposed that, rather than the traditionalist d’Indy, Vaughan Williams should take lessons with his close friend Maurice Ravel, by then one of the most admired young composers in France.

The two men could hardly have been more different: Ravel petite, fastidious, intensely private, an avid collector of intricate mechanical toys; Vaughan Williams bulky, dishevelled, bluffly nonconformist, and possessed of a fascination for English folk music that Ravel found incomprehensible. But though they got off to a poor start (in their first lesson Ravel set Vaughan Williams to compose a little minuet in the style of Mozart, an exercise the Englishman refused in no uncertain terms to consider), the three months they spent together in Paris marked the start of a friendship that would profoundly touch both men and their music.

In a recent interview, Jonathan Coe admitted that “ever since I discovered that my two favourite composers … were friends and supporters of each other, I’ve wanted to write a novel about them”. Their music clearly delights him – the book comes with a splendid playlist – but what surely made this story irresistible to Coe, that great chronicler of Englishness, was how both Vaughan Williams and Ravel came, in their work, to embody something quintessential about their respective countries. Widely celebrated for its clarity, elegance and formal emotional control, Ravel’s music exemplifies the pinnacle of French cultural values, while Vaughan Williams drew on ancient hymns, chorales and folk music to create work in a consciously English tradition. “‘Englishry’ is in the very blood and bones of his music,” the Times declared in 1952, an assessment supported by Ravel, who described his friend as “a real artist, who only realised his richness when he learned to be English!”

Lessons in Harmony takes the form of an unpublished memoir written by Ravel’s devoted friend Pierre “Mylo” Mylonas, loosely based on Calvocoressi, after Ravel’s death, and “discovered” accidentally decades later. Coe, himself an accomplished musician, has described the book as a fantasia, a freeform composition that does not follow strict traditional structures, and the novel has all of the exhilarating immediacy of improvisation, shifting suddenly in tempo and mood, modulating frequently to unexpected keys. An inserted section written by another of Ravel’s pupils about a visit to London that Mylo had to miss is interpolated with Mylo’s exasperated corrections, while a virtuoso vignette involving the shifting of a piano might have come straight from Buster Keaton.

Lessons in Harmony is the story of an unlikely and transformative friendship. It is also a masterful examination of national identity and how it shapes us. Mylo, born to a Portuguese father and Greek mother, shuttling between London and Paris, is a man without a homeland, an often penniless polyglot moored by a single fixed point: his private passion for Ravel. Beneath the surface of his beguilingly partisan account lies a mesh of conflicting dualities: of nature and artifice, tradition and modernity, slapstick and seriousness, egoism and generosity of spirit, selfhood and country. Ravel and Vaughan Williams may remain as chalk and cheese but, as the understanding between them deepens, and works its way into their music, the lines between them soften and blur. Mylo himself is altered by the changes in them – opened up. It is only with the advent of the first world war, with national identity hardened and pressed into the service of mass slaughter, that the connection stutters, redrawing borders and forcing a retreat.

Ravel and Vaughan Williams both served in that terrible conflict, Ravel in the trenches and Vaughan Williams as an ambulance driver. They fought on the same side, facing the same enemy, but, though they remained in touch, their friendship never quite recovered. Two decades later the world was at war once again. In the opening pages of Coe’s subtly tender and generous novel, Vaughan Williams asks his friend Evans if he thinks it is possible for music to represent the soul of a nation. At its close, as Mylo recalls the triumphant premiere of his Fifth Symphony at the Proms of 1943, the opinion of the critics is a resounding yes. In the darkness of war, Vaughan Williams stands as a beacon of hope, an expression of a deep shared Englishness, an inspiration and a benediction. Whether great music can ever be that simply categorised, and whether indeed we who listen to it can hope to live up to so noble an ideal of nationhood, Coe leaves it to us to judge.

entries.title: Killing the Pope review – the truth behind the attempted murder of John Paul II
entries.summary: Was the failed assassination of the Polish pope a Soviet plot or simply the work of a deranged hitman?On the afternoon of Wednesday 13 May 1981, St Peter’s Square in Rome was packed with more than 10,000 pilgrims, excited to see the charismatic John Paul II, formerly Karol Wojtyla, archbishop of Kraków. Two and a half years earlier he had become the youngest cardinal to be elected pope in more tha
entries.content:
On the afternoon of Wednesday 13 May 1981, St Peter’s Square in Rome was packed with more than 10,000 pilgrims, excited to see the charismatic John Paul II, formerly Karol Wojtyla, archbishop of Kraków. Two and a half years earlier he had become the youngest cardinal to be elected pope in more than a century and the first non-Italian for 455 years.

At 5.17pm a man pulled out a concealed pistol and raised it with both hands above the heads of the crowd. He took aim at the pope, only a few metres away, and fired several shots. Then, as he backed away from the shocked bystanders, he tripped and fell, where he lay pinned to the ground by a Franciscan nun until handcuffed by uniformed police. Meanwhile the pope had been hit by two bullets, one in the arm and the other in the abdomen. He was losing blood rapidly. He was rushed to hospital and underwent an operation, before beginning a slow recovery. The would-be assassin was soon revealed to be Mehmet Ali Ağca, a member of the rightwing Turkish paramilitary group known as the Grey Wolves.

Almost immediately speculation began that Ağca had not been acting alone. In his new book, Serhii Plokhy weighs the claim, first made in an Italian court, that the assassin had been “only the visible point of a conspiracy”. Plokhy has previously written several highly praised works, including Chernobyl: History of a Tragedy, which won the 2018 Baillie Gifford prize. He has a deserved reputation for careful research and reasoned evaluation.

Of several competing theories, the one that gained most traction was that Ağca was a tool of Bulgarian state security, acting on behalf of their Soviet masters. This is what the CIA came to believe, despite their initial scepticism. Plokhy himself admits that he set out feeling more sympathetic towards the proponents of the “Bulgarian connection” than to their opponents. There was a strong case to be made: the pope was in the frontline of the cold war. He was a Pole, Poland was overwhelmingly Catholic, and the church represented a challenge to communist rule.

In 1979, only nine months after being elected, John Paul II had made a visit to his homeland and had celebrated mass in the centre of Warsaw, in front of an audience of 300,000 Soon the Catholic church was providing financial and moral support to the new unofficial trade union, Solidarity, which was rapidly becoming a focus of civil resistance to the regime. In January 1981 Solidarity’s leader, Lech Wałęsa, had visited Rome and enjoyed a private audience with the pope. There was no doubt that the pressure for change in Poland caused deep concern in Moscow; the Russians threatened to invade if the Polish authorities didn’t suppress the uprising themselves.

And if the Russians doubted the power of a religious leader to cause political upheaval, they only had to look to Iran, where the return of Ayatollah Khomeini in 1979 had brought about the overthrow of a western-backed regime previously assumed to be stable. As for the Bulgarians, they had form: in 1978 they had employed an agent to assassinate Georgi Markov, a Bulgarian dissident in London, using a poisoned umbrella to stab him as he waited for a bus on Waterloo Bridge.

Hardline anti-communist embraced the theory uncritically. Yet one might equally well argue that, far from wanting him out of the way, the Soviet leadership needed the pope as a restraining influence on the Polish insurgency. An article in the official Russian newspaper Izvestiia argued instead that the Americans were responsible for the assassination through their funding neo-fascist and terrorist groups in Turkey.

Plokhy, for his part, has found no evidence of an international conspiracy, and changed his mind about “the Bulgarian connection”. In that sense the book is an anticlimax: there was no smoking gun, except the Browning dropped by Ağca in St Peter’s Square. Plokhy’s downbeat conclusion is that Ağca, like most assassins, was probably just another deranged individual seeking notoriety.

Ağca’s testimony during his interrogation and trial was contradictory and sometimes palpably false. To the neutral observer it was obvious that he was bargaining for a reduced sentence. Some of his claims were so fantastic as to lead the Italian magistrates to doubt his sanity. “I am Jesus Christ!” he shouted from his steel cage in the courtroom to reporters and cameramen gathered for the trial of his alleged Bulgarian accomplices, who were acquitted. Nevertheless people believed what they wanted to believe. The pope himself was convinced from the start that the KGB was behind the assassination attempt. In an act of extraordinary forgiveness, John Paul visited Ağca in prison and spent 20 minutes in private conversation with him.

John Paul II died in 2005. Ağca issued a statement from prison mourning the death of his “spiritual brother”, the man whom he had tried to kill. He was released in 2010. On 27 December 2014, 31 years to the day after the pope had visited him in prison, Ağca stood in front of John Paul’s tomb in the Vatican, and after a few moments of apparent silent meditation, laid some white roses there. For this stunt he was accompanied by a television crew.

Plokhy writes in clear, straight­forward prose. He has opted to use the present tense throughout and while this technique works well for the period immediately following the assassination, injecting an immediacy to the narrative, it is less effective and occasionally confusing when describing more recent events. Nevertheless, in telling this bizarre – at times even grotesque – story, he holds the reader’s attention to the end.

entries.title: Look at Me by Dustin Hoffman review – an era-defining actor says his piece
entries.summary: At 89, the star of the Graduate and Rain Man demonstrates both brilliance and a startling lack of self-awarenessThe choice of title for an actor’s autobiography can be revealing. Sylvester Stallone went with The Steps, conflating life’s challenging progress with those steps at the Philadelphia Museum of Art that Rocky euphorically ran up. Michael Douglas cheerfully and unreflectively called his On
entries.content:
The choice of title for an actor’s autobiography can be revealing. Sylvester Stallone went with The Steps, conflating life’s challenging progress with those steps at the Philadelphia Museum of Art that Rocky euphorically ran up. Michael Douglas cheerfully and unreflectively called his One Helluva Ride.

Dustin Hoffman’s is one of those that harks back to the poignantly vulnerable youthful world in which the acting bug first took effect. Al Pacino called his Sonny Boy; Anthony Hopkins gave us We Did OK, Kid. Hoffman’s Look at Me is about the yearning to be seen and heard. Or is it about a childish impulse to show off?

On location for the thriller Marathon Man in 1975, playing the regular guy unforgettably finding himself in a Nazi war-criminal’s dentist chair, Hoffman told co-star Laurence Olivier that acting was all about having something to say to the world. “Bollocks,” Olivier crisply replied – and then explained the acting impulse by putting his face close to Dustin and whispering: “Look at me, look at me, look at me, look at me, look at me.”

Well, first things first. Any reader of Hoffman’s autobiography will want to know the truth behind another legendary anecdote involving Olivier. Did he really stay up all night in a solemn method-acting inspired bid to look exhausted, only to be told by Larry: “Try acting, dear boy”?

Sadly, the answer is no. And Hoffman’s explanation exposes the sneaky journalistic trick of stripping the intentional irony out of someone else’s story, and re-applying it at the author’s expense. Hoffman had been up all night, yes, partying and doing coke at Studio 54; he showed up for work looking terrible. Olivier, amused and unshocked, humorously told him to try acting – and the Vanity Fair journalist to whom Hoffman told this rewrote it to make him look like a ridiculous prig.

This book is ghosted by New Yorker staff writer Ariel Levy, and perhaps in imitation of the manner in which Hoffman spoke into Levy’s recording device, the story jumps grasshopper-like back and forth along the timeline. There are two deeply painful things that stand out: Hoffman’s dad and Hoffman’s exposure to the #MeToo movement. We hear a lot about the first, hardly anything about the second.

Hoffman was the smart, scrappy underdog, the livewire kid from the secular Jewish home in California whose mum tried to persuade him at 12 years old to get a nose job, at the same time as she was getting hers. He took acting classes in college for extra credit and, instantly addicted to laughs and applause, came out east to make it in the excitingly high-minded world of New York theatre. He hung out with fellow young hopefuls Gene Hackman and Robert Duvall, themselves seething and simmering with displaced ambition and anger. Hoffman was destined to be a standard-bearer for the gritty American new wave in which leading actors were allowed to be more rough-looking (although this dispensation did not apply to women).

The brilliant young comedian and director Mike Nichols sensationally cast this Broadway up-and-comer against type (people expected a Robert Redford figure) as the young man seduced by an older woman in The Graduate, which functioned as a vivid metaphor for the new cinema and the old.

Hoffman was 30 and made up to look younger; his co-star Anne Bancroft was 36 and lit to look older, a sexist imbalance that didn’t fully register with him at the time. But something jarred when he read the Mad magazine spoof of his Graduate character: “Mom, how come I’m Jewish and you and dad aren’t?” Antisemitism played a nasty little part in much of the mockery he periodically endured from the press in those days, ostensibly for not being sufficiently tall and handsome.

The Graduate had been Hoffman’s last chance at a juve lead. Then he was the dishevelled, disabled grifter Ratso Rizzo in John Schlesinger’s Midnight Cowboy, limping along behind Jon Voight, screaming “I’m walkin’ here!” at a New York cab that bumped into him – a line he improvised, because Hoffman really was passionately devoted to being in the moment, method style, a dedication that fascinated and disconcerted costars like Meryl Streep and Tom Cruise. And, like Gene Hackman, he was difficult and in the habit of talking back to the director.

He was the tough guy in Ulu Grosbard’s crime thriller Straight Time; the adorable dad in Kramer vs Kramer, which became a water cooler moment and dinner party talking point from coast to coast; the disguised woman in Tootsie; the bleary movie producer in Wag the Dog (not based on Paramount Pictures’ supremo Robert Evans, he says, contrary to popular myth); and the autistic savant brother in Rain Man, opposite Tom Cruise – a fascinating pairing of two performers laser-focused in different ways. It was a part he had based on Peter Guthrie, the autistic brother of all-American Princeton football star Kevin Guthrie. But Hoffman appears genially unaware of the contemporary issues of gender politics and authentic casting that might now colour the reception of some of these portrayals.

The star of this book, in fact its tragic hero, is Hoffman’s angry and opinionated dad, Harry, who had himself longed for Hollywood success and was unreconciled to Dustin’s. He had been head of the prop department at Columbia Pictures and worked on Frank Capra’s Mr Smith Goes to Washington – but got fired for talking back to his superiors in the way Dustin was just about allowed to do a generation later. Hoffman Sr opened a furniture store and angrily – abusively – took his frustrations out on his sons, Ronny and Dusty.

There is a Dickensian melancholy to the story Hoffman tells about his dad being allowed to come and watch filming of The Graduate. Afterwards, Dustin found the director hilariously regaling everyone with how this absurd man, Harry, had come out from behind the rope and presumed to tell Mr Nichols how to shoot the scene. The humiliation of that is perhaps something Dustin still hasn’t quite processed, although he says he based his stage portrayal of Willy Loman in Arthur Miller’s Death of a Salesman on his father, with mannerisms that he thought Harry would surely recognise. But Harry came backstage to his dressing room and said: “Wow! That guy is some loser …” Did that mean Harry really hadn’t seen the resemblance? I wonder.

And so to Hoffman being accused, in 2017, of having groped and sexually harassed 17-year-old intern Anna Graham Hunter on the set of the TV movie adaptation of his Death of a Salesman production in 1985, which was followed by his Salesman co-star on Broadway, Kathryn Rossetter, making similar accusations, and two other women, Cori Thomas and Melissa Kester, coming forward. Hoffman denied any wrongdoing but conceded thoughtless, tactless behaviour. But none of this is specifically discussed in the book; no names are mentioned, the issue dispatched in a couple of pages. Of #MeToo, he recalls the “reckoning … making its way around the internet”, which he says he welcomed. And then: “Suddenly, my entire life changed.”

He doesn’t say how, in detail, other than to compare himself to a victim of McCarthyism, and to write that “things were being said about me that just weren’t true”. He asks sonorously: “Is it possible that I’ve been guilty of insufficient empathy? That I was too self-involved to correctly perceive what the people around me were feeling at the time? Sure. Of course.” Well, his accusers alleged something more specific than that.

Dustin Hoffman is a garrulous, grandfatherly, un-self-aware figure in this book, a brilliant, intuitive, era-defining screen actor. Perhaps his continued need to work, and not to fade into retirement as he reaches the end of his 80s, is partly due to a desire to see off those accusations, to ensure they aren’t the last thing in the story.

entries.title: Two Women by Jacqueline Rose review – a memorial to Gillian Rose
entries.summary: The connections between the author’s sister and the German Jewish philosopher Edith Stein are vividly imagined in alternating chapters of a fictional biographyIn a long and distinguished career as a feminist cultural critic, Jacqueline Rose has combined psychoanalysis, politics, human rights and literature in her work. Among her books are The Haunting of Sylvia Plath and Women in Dark Times, and a
entries.content:
In a long and distinguished career as a feminist cultural critic, Jacqueline Rose has combined psychoanalysis, politics, human rights and literature in her work. Among her books are The Haunting of Sylvia Plath and Women in Dark Times, and a novel, 2001’s Albertine, focusing on Albertine Simonet, a character from Proust’s In Search of Lost Time. Her second novel, Two Women, similarly draws on biography and, in this case, memoir, to explore the lives of Edith Stein, the German Jewish philosopher turned Carmelite nun who was murdered in Auschwitz in 1942, and Gillian Rose, Jacqueline’s older sister, a sociologist and philosopher who died of ovarian cancer in 1995, aged just 48.

On her deathbed, Gillian converted from Judaism to the Anglican church, a journey outlined in her slim, elaborately erudite and gorgeously frank memoir, Love’s Work. The book gained cult and then classic status, and is probably better known than her radical philosophical works such as Hegel Contra Sociology, although it is comparable to all her output as a manifesto on how to suffer and how to live. Like Stein, Gillian felt a deep frustration that her groundbreaking work as a philosopher would not be recognised in her lifetime. In the case of Stein, a phenomenologist who studied under Edmund Husserl and was doubly thwarted by being a woman and a Jew in Nazi Germany, posthumous ascendancy to sainthood took the place of professional accolades in life. She was canonised by Pope John Paul II in 1998. When she made her perpetual vows in 1938, a quote from St John of the Cross adorned Stein’s devotional picture: “Henceforth my only vocation is to love.”

While grounded, intimate and relatable, there is also an element of the mystical in Gillian Rose’s memoir, and Rose goes some way towards beatifying her sister while working through the pain of loss. Impressively, if at times heavy-handedly, Two Women imagines an interconnection between Gillian and Stein in the form of a fictionalised chronological biography, alternating chapters of the two women’s lives. She begins with the sudden death of Stein’s timber merchant father near Breslau in 1893, when Edith, the youngest of 11 children, was two. From that point Edith’s redoubtable mother took charge of the family business, despite her now “vexed and flattened” world.

In the novel Edith is renamed Esther Felsenstein; Gillian is Rosa Edelblum, and her sister is Clara. Rosa and Clara grow up in a middle-class family in postwar west London with a younger half-sister. The children of a bitter divorce, and semi-estranged from their father, they take their stepfather’s surname. Born 20 months apart, Rosa seems always to have been the leader, the rebel: “for Rosa, childhood was an insult … a waiting room to a more intelligent world”.

In Breslau, Esther rejects the Judaism of her family for atheism in the same way that she turns away from marriage and motherhood. She breaks off her studies in 1915 to nurse for the Red Cross: “nothing could have prepared her for the human mind and body in their most raw, vulnerable, at moments, amoral state”. Each experience is a step toward the Catholicism she will eventually embrace.

While Rose’s depiction of Esther/Edith is deeply researched and visualised, her account of the close sisterhood of Rosa and Clara is of course the product of memory. There is a wonderful moment in which the two academic young women, “born mid-century, the offshoots of a genocide about which they were meant to know nothing”, contemplate their futures as they sit on an autumn lawn in the late 1960s at St Hilda’s, Oxford, the all-women college at which they have both ended up. Rosa in particular has escaped family strife and disapproval: but from this point “she would uncouple herself from disaster by staring it unblinking in the face”. In 1990, Gillian Rose was selected as a consultant on the Polish committee for the future of Auschwitz.

As war and antisemitic pogroms take hold, Esther does not flee. The mass roundup of Jews begins in mid 1941 and from then convents are emptied of any nun who is a convert from Judaism.Esther and her sister Rahel, who has followed her into the Catholic church, are sent by convoy to their fate one August morning: “towards God, Esther believed and prayed – they stepped one foot at a time into each other’s tread”. For the second set of sisters, once Rosa receives her terminal diagnosis, there is also very little time. Levity is almost entirely absent in this book – even an impromptu LSD trip in 1970s New York is treated with the utmost gravity. But we end with the pair, determinedly in high heels, on a final trip in France to see the famous sculpture of Christ carved over the tympanum of the basilica at Vézelay. “Clara had brought Rosa all this way as an act of love.” Ultimately Two Women is just that: an act of love, a memorial of faith.

Two Women by Jacqueline Rose is published by Fitzcarraldo (£14.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.content:
If you ever find yourself in an airport newsagent, it might be worth peering inside one of Liz Pichon’s books. “I do guerrilla signings,” she tells me conspiratorially. “They let me go in and I sign all the books, just in case. I love the idea of kids buying a book, going on holiday and seeing that I’ve signed it. Sometimes I write ‘surprise!’”

It’s a wonder that she hasn’t got sore hands. Pichon is one of the UK’s foremost children’s authors, and this is a big year for her. Not only has she just published the 25th book in her Tom Gates series, Tom Gates Is Not Famous (Yet), but this is the 15th anniversary of the first instalment. She has, at last count, sold 16.5m books in 47 languages, and her work has been adapted for both stage and screen.

“I can’t believe it’s 15 years since the first one came out,” she says on a video call from her home. “Now I get 19- and 20-year-olds that grew up with my books. They’ll turn up at an event with a big stack of them and go ‘these were my favourites’, which makes me feel very old.”

Although by no means Pichon’s only project – her comic book series The Mubbles is going from strength to strength – Tom Gates seems more and more like her life’s work. A decade and a half is a long time to maintain any series, let alone one in which the main character has been at the same school all along. But the magic of Tom Gates is that the books never feel as if they’re covering old ground. The stories (usually about Tom’s scrapes with his best friend, Derek, older sister Delia and irritating classmate Marcus Meldrew) remain fresh, while the presentation – scrappy, handmade, packed with bonus content and extra features – is just as endearing as ever.

“There’s always that moment of slight panic when you first start, where you think: ‘What am I going to write about this time? What haven’t I covered?’” she says. “But I write about small details of family life, things that might happen at home and school, with friends and pets. There’s always something that comes up.”

The newest book is based on something that once happened to her husband, songwriter and producer Mark Flannery, who spent his early career as a studio runner for U2. “He told me a story about how he was trying to go to a Simple Minds concert with a friend and they couldn’t get in,” she says. “All of a sudden this big limo pulls up, and U2 get out. The drummer goes, ‘Mark come with us, we’ll get you in.’ I always thought that would be a fun plot for a book.”

Pichon enjoys a weird kind of success. Unlike those who write for adults, whose readers might stay with them for a lifetime, children’s authors only have their followers for a short stretch before they grow up and move on. As such, Tom Gates has managed to entertain a rolling caravan of new fans, which is astoundingly hard to maintain. Pichon puts this down to her refusal to cater to modern tastes.

“There’s not much technology,” she explains. “You won’t get much text messaging or anything like that. There are some things in childhood that just don’t change. Sibling rivalries, stuff like that. Children in different territories enjoy reading these books, and I think maybe one reason is because I’m not very specific, so they can really put themselves into the setting.”

Now 63, Pichon grew up in London and lives in Brighton. She didn’t start writing until she was in her mid-40s, having previously worked designing album covers for Jive Records and a range of greetings cards, and then illustrating picture books for other writers. The late start is something she puts down to insecurity over her dyslexia as a child. “I came from a generation where people just thought I wasn’t academic,” she says. “Of all the things I was good at, none of them were considered to be things you could actually make a living from. So you grow up with that in the background, a lack of expectation. I didn’t have a clue what I wanted to do.”

Tom Gates came from what she describes as a desire to start making things she was genuinely proud of. The first was created in an exercise book, full of handwritten diary-style text and visuals. “I took all the things I’d learned in picture books, like grabby page turns, and used them for a slightly older audience,” she says. The result was her signature style with ideas tumbling out in sketches, sight gags and bonus content. (The latest contains a short script that readers can act out with their friends, and songs she has written for the book can be found on streaming platforms.) “Kids get into the stories really quickly because the presentation is so accessible,” she says.

“I’m passionate about this,” Pichon continues. “When I do school visits, we talk about things that are happening in the kids’ lives, and how they can get those stories out of their heads. I show them how I tell stories with drawings and doodles and things. Hopefully when they leave, they’re not only excited about reading the books, but actually going on to be creative themselves. We all tell stories in different ways. Some kids will feel like they can’t draw, or can’t write, or aren’t very good at spelling, and this gives them a way to feel like they’re being seen and heard and celebrated.”

A core part of Pichon’s audience is what some would dub “reluctant readers”, although she prefers the term “unconfident”; youngsters who need a visual element to suck them into a story. “They just need a book that gets them in,” she says. “Once they’re in, they’re readers.” The visuals of Pichon’s books – plus the fact that they’re incredibly funny, and can be read for pure enjoyment – have meant that she has amassed something of a rarity in these times; an audience largely composed of boys.

“Honestly, it wasn’t something I set out to do,” she says. “I created Tom Gates because I just kept on drawing that little character’s face. When I started, boys would be quite surprised, because there weren’t that many women writing in that genre. But I’m not writing for boys or girls. I’m just writing stuff that I think I would enjoy. I write about relationships where everyone generally gets on. There’s a bit of snarkiness, but they’re not mean to each other. I hope the books are just a nice place to be.”

Given the milestones, and the enormous sales, you might expect that Pichon would be tempted to rest on her laurels a little, but not a bit of it. As well as forging ahead with The Mubbles, it seems as though there is no end in sight for Tom Gates. “I’m still learning, all the time,” Pichon says. “Do you remember being a kid and really liking a series of books? You could tell if they started dialling it in, don’t you think? So at this stage, although I’ve got a new batch of readers, I still feel like, you’re only as good as your last book. You just can’t take your readers for granted.”
